cpau:cc-e-14-2025-07-01: The Section C rate table of the published Schedule E-14 is fully represented: all seventeen fixture ratings (the 400 watt mercury-vapor lamp, four high pressure sodium vapor ratings, five LED ratings and seven traffic signal and speed sign types) are priced, as is the Section D.2 switching surcharge of $2.50 per month. What is not represented is the conditions the schedule attaches to those rates. Section A limits the schedule to street and highway lighting installations at service voltages from 120 to 480, and this filing's eligibility rule states no voltage condition. Section D.2 makes the switching surcharge conditional twice over, waiving it where each separately switched circuit carries at least 10 kilowatts of lamp load and waiving it again where the switching installation is made for CPAU's convenience; the 10 kilowatt threshold survives only in the name of the metric the charge counts and the convenience waiver only in prose, so a consumer computing a bill has to apply both by hand. Section D.3 conditions the whole rate table on the lamps running to a CPAU-approved burning schedule not exceeding 4,100 hours per year, which is likewise prose. Section D.5 is a hole in the price list rather than a missing condition: a customer who installs a lamp rating not on the schedule is billed at an interim rate CPAU prepares from its own estimated costs until that rating is added, and no such rate is published, so the eighteen prices here are not exhaustive of what an E-14 bill can carry. Two further Section D provisions are out of scope rather than missing: D.1's rule that the customer bears the cost of underground connections is a construction cost and not a rate, and D.4's maintenance terms describe what the per-lamp rate already includes.
cpau:cc-e-3-2007-07-01: Both published buyback tables are represented: Section C.1 for facilities without an interval meter, at $0.07902 per kWh in summer and $0.07831 in winter with a $4.32 per kW-month capacity credit available to firm power only, and Section C.2 for facilities with an interval meter, all five time-of-use energy cells plus the peak-period firm capacity credit in each season. Section C.3 is not represented. It lets a facility rated above 1 MW request a market-based buyback instead, equal to the City's average cost of electricity at the PG&E City Gate for energy and capacity purchased at the first of the month together with daily market prices for that month, bounded at $2.00 to $10.00 per kW-month and $0.03 to $0.20 per kWh for firm power and at $0.03 to $0.20 per kWh with no capacity component for non-firm. Neither that reference price nor its bounds appear anywhere in the filing, so a consumer pricing a facility above 1 MW that has elected it will find only the Section C.1 or C.2 rate here. Two further provisions publish no number to model: Section D sets transmission rates site by site on a case by case basis, and Section E.2 requires the quantity of power delivered to be adjusted for losses and for administrative costs without stating a factor. Section E.3's settlement rule is not represented either. Under it the generation credit computed from these rates is applied against the customer's own monthly charge for electric service, and the utility pays the customer the balance in the months when credits exceed that charge; this filing prices the buyback and carries no netting or cash-out step. Section E.5 is out of scope rather than missing: the utility reserves the right to charge for facilities it holds on standby for the customer's load, but places that charge in the customer's service contract rather than in this schedule, so there is no published rate to model.
cpau:cc-e-2-g-2025-07-01: The published Schedule E-2-G offers two ways into the Palo Alto Green Program and this filing represents one of them. Section C.1, the 100% Renewable Option, is modeled as the $0.0075 per kWh Palo Alto Green Charge that rides on every kWh consumed; the commodity, distribution and public benefits components printed alongside it are Schedule E-2's own values, republished unchanged, and are carried by the cpau:e-2 base filing rather than duplicated here. Section C.2, the 1000 kWh Block Purchase Option, is not represented. A customer on that option pays no per-kWh green adder at all and instead asks CPAU to buy a designated number of discrete 1,000 kWh blocks of renewable energy credits at $7.50 per block, a count of blocks the customer requests and may revise in writing at any time rather than a quantity the meter produces, so there is nothing in this filing to price such a customer with. Two Section D provisions are out of scope rather than missing: the D.4 maximum demand meter rule, under which a demand meter is installed once monthly use has exceeded 8,000 kWh for three consecutive months and may be removed once it has fallen below 6,000 kWh for twelve, is a metering operation and not a rate, and the Palo Alto Green Program application and change procedure in D.3 is a customer service step.
cpau:cc-e-4-g-2025-07-01: This filing carries only what the Palo Alto Green Program adds to Schedule E-4: the $0.0075 per kWh Palo Alto Green Charge of Section C.1, the 100% Renewable Option. Section C.2, the 1000 kWh Block Purchase Option, is not represented. A customer on that option pays no per-kWh green adder and instead has CPAU buy a designated number of 1,000 kWh blocks of renewable energy credits at $7.50 per block, requested and revised in writing under Section D.5, which is a count of blocks rather than metered consumption, so there is nothing here to price such a customer with. Everything else the published Schedule E-4-G prints is Schedule E-4 restated: the summer and winter commodity, distribution and public benefits energy components, the two-part demand charge and the $126.24 monthly customer charge carry the same values as the cpau:e-4 base filing, and the Section D special notes are E-4's. Three of those notes are unmodeled in the base as well, so a consumer who composes this modifier onto cpau:e-4 still will not have them: D.6 Primary Voltage Discount, 2.5 percent for customers taking service at the supply line voltage above 2 kV; D.8 Standby Charge, $46.58 per kW of reserved capacity in summer and $23.49 in winter for customers with a non-utility generation source on their side of the revenue meter, together with its maximum demand credit and its exemptions for backup-only generators and for eligible customer-generators under Public Utilities Code Section 2827(b)(4); and the D.3 exception under which billing demand for Thermal Energy Storage customers is taken from the noon to 6 PM weekday window rather than from all hours. The rest of D.3, the demand meter installation rule and the City's option to measure over a 5-minute interval or with a thermal-type meter, is out of scope rather than missing, being a metering operation and not a rate, as is the D.4 right to request a change of rate schedule.
cpau:cc-e-7-g-2025-07-01: This filing carries only what the Palo Alto Green Program adds to Schedule E-7: the $0.0075 per kWh Palo Alto Green Charge of Section C.1, the 100% Renewable Option. Section C.2, the 1000 kWh Block Purchase Option, is not represented. A customer on that option pays no per-kWh green adder and instead has CPAU buy a designated number of 1,000 kWh blocks of renewable energy credits at $7.50 per block, requested and revised in writing under Section D.6, which is a count of blocks rather than metered consumption, so there is nothing here to price such a customer with. Everything else the published Schedule E-7-G prints is Schedule E-7 restated: the summer and winter commodity, distribution and public benefits energy components, the two-part demand charge and the $578.08 monthly customer charge carry the same values as the cpau:e-7 base filing, and the Section D special notes are E-7's. Four of those notes are unmodeled in the base as well, so a consumer who composes this modifier onto cpau:e-7 still will not have them: D.7 Primary Voltage Discount, 2.8 percent for customers taking service at the supply line voltage above 2 kV; D.9 Standby Charge, $40.79 per kW of reserved capacity in summer and $27.75 in winter for customers with a non-utility generation source on their side of the revenue meter, together with its maximum demand credit and its exemptions for backup-only generators and for eligible customer-generators under Public Utilities Code Section 2827(b)(4); the D.3 exception under which billing demand for Thermal Energy Storage customers is taken from the noon to 6 PM weekday window rather than from all hours; and D.4 Request for Service, which lets a qualifying customer take service under this schedule for more than one account or meter where the accounts cover contiguous parcels with no intervening public right-of-way and share a common billing address, an aggregation URPX v0.5.1 gives no site or account class to scope. The rest of D.3, the demand meter installation rule and the City's option to measure over a 5-minute interval or with a thermal-type meter, is out of scope rather than missing, being a metering operation and not a rate, as is the D.5 right to request a change of rate schedule.
